story.title: Knowing both facts is not the same as combining them
paragraphs: Retrieval often supplies only the missing part of an answer, and the model must connect it with parametric knowledge, the facts stored in its weights. This differs from deciding whether to trust a passage that contradicts memory: both sources are correct, but neither suffices alone. EchoQA tests this complementary case alongside supportive, conflicting, and irrelevant context.
A correct answer does not prove composition either: without context, a model can infer an artificial entity's properties from its name and then eliminate answer options.

mechanism.title: Each model is tested only on facts it already knows
paragraphs: EchoQA first asks each model the underlying fact directly and keeps only facts it answers correctly; the context then supplies a different, necessary fact. A later failure therefore cannot come from a missing prerequisite. Questions are multiple choice with an explicit Unknown option, so the unknown-answer rate (U_R) measures abstention on questions the model has the knowledge to answer.

Instructions are progressively enforced. The Neutral Instruction (NI) already asks the model to combine the information with its own knowledge; Trust Yourself (TYI) adds that the information is insufficient, or that the model should prefer its own knowledge under conflict; Speak Out Loud (SOLI) makes it state that knowledge first. A golden-knowledge condition puts every needed fact in the context.

Each relationship demands different behavior: keep a known fact against fabricated context, combine both sources when they complement each other, and ignore irrelevant context. No fixed preference for memory or context satisfies all three.

evidence.title: Complementary context raises abstention on known facts
paragraphs: The pattern is not specific to one model. With complementary scientific context and the neutral instruction, the unknown-answer rate rises above its no-context level for every tested model except OpenAI o1, and at least doubles for the Llama and Qwen models. Writing all required facts into the context lowers it for every model, so the difficulty lies in drawing on memory once context is present.

In 200 random Llama 3.1-70B failures, questions it answered alone but missed with complementary context, the model relied only on the context and answer choices in 93.5% of cases. The authors hypothesize that instruction tuning, which trains answers from either context or memory, contributes to this behavior.
